articles.title: We built a pipeline that makes a market show twice a day. The first episode aired on schedule.
articles.excerpt: Yesterday our news app published a morning briefing and an evening briefing, like it does every day. Today it added a second show on top of that: StarBrook Business, twice a day. A midday market repor…
articles.body: Yesterday our news app published a morning briefing and an evening briefing, like it does every day. Today it added a second show on top of that: StarBrook Business, twice a day. A midday market report at 11:30 AM Central, and a market-close wrap at 3:00 PM Central. Ninety seconds each, vertical, same voice and same look as the briefings. The first live episode went out today, Tuesday, November 24, on schedule. It was built by a pipeline, not by a person sitting down to edit: scheduled execution, story selection, market data, narration, validation, assembly, storage, publication, distribution. Nobody touched it between the cron firing and the video landing in the app. That's the story. The pipeline worked.
articles.author: Matthew Douglas

articles.title: Writing .ics files by hand in vanilla JS: the 5 bugs I hit (octet folding, all-day alarms, stable UIDs)
articles.excerpt: I built a small browser-only tool that turns a list of subscriptions into calendar reminders for "cancel by" dates. No library, no server: the page builds the .ics text itself and hands it to the brow…
articles.body: I built a small browser-only tool that turns a list of subscriptions into calendar reminders for "cancel by" dates. No library, no server: the page builds the .ics text itself and hands it to the browser as a download. RFC 5545 looks simple until you test the output in a strict parser. Here are the five things that broke, and the fixes. 1. Line folding counts octets, not characters RFC 5545 says content lines SHOULD NOT be longer than 75 octets , excluding the line break. Longer lines are folded with CRLF followed by a single space. "abc".length counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes. A Japanese or emoji subscription name blows past 75 bytes while .length still says 40.

articles.title: Cacti Zero-Day: Guest Access Lets Attackers Run Commands on the Server. Is Your Monitoring Panel Open?
articles.excerpt: Many web servers run more than the website. A hosting company or a developer often adds a monitoring panel next to the site, so they can watch traffic, disk space and uptime on graphs. Cacti is one of…
articles.body: Many web servers run more than the website. A hosting company or a developer often adds a monitoring panel next to the site, so they can watch traffic, disk space and uptime on graphs. Cacti is one of the best known open-source tools for that job. This week, a Cacti zero-day with a public exploit showed how that helper can become a way in. On 26 November 2026, a researcher who goes by ek0ms savi0r published a working attack chain on GitHub and named it 4HTTP2SHELL (first called 4HTTP2ROOT). According to the researcher, four ordinary web requests take a visitor with no login to running commands on the Cacti server. There was no fix when it went public. According to BleepingComputer, the researcher said they did not report the flaw to Cacti first.
articles.author: HackerMe

articles.title: 96 breaches, one checklist: making coding agents check for old mistakes
articles.excerpt: Your AI wrote the login page. Did it also write the GitLab bug? In January 2023 security researchers found that GitLab's password reset accepted more than one email address. The reset link went to the…
articles.body: Your AI wrote the login page. Did it also write the GitLab bug? Most breaches are old mistakes made again. I turned 96 of them into a checklist your coding agent can run. In January 2023 security researchers found that GitLab's password reset accepted more than one email address. The reset link went to the account's real address, and also to the one the attacker added. In 2022 Optus served customer records from an API where the record ID was all you needed. In 2019 Capital One's server was persuaded to fetch an internal URL, which handed over cloud credentials. In 2025, apps built with AI app builders shipped databases without row-level security, so the public key in the browser could read every row. None of these needed a new kind of attack. Each one was a known mistake, made again.

articles.title: One bad number almost shipped in our markets line. So we made two sources agree first.
articles.excerpt: Our news app publishes a markets line in every evening edition — S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq, one line, right at the top of the Business section. It's a small line. It is also the line most likely to be wron…
articles.body: Our news app publishes a markets line in every evening edition — S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq, one line, right at the top of the Business section. It's a small line. It is also the line most likely to be wrong, because it comes from a single API call to a single vendor, and nobody checks the answer before it ships. Last week my bar for that line was three words: free, reliable, independent. Free, because the news is free and the budget for this is zero. Reliable, because a wrong number in a news product is worse than no number. Independent, because one vendor's word is not a fact — it's a claim. No single free source passed all three. Yahoo's finance API is free and current, but on its own it fails "independent." Stooq, the other free option, was dead when we tested it.

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.

(The parade has been postponed two days from Thursday, Nov. 26, due to bad weather.) Not that Macy's (or the space agency) has hinted about anything cosmic planned for the 100th parade; it's only that the event has had a long history of celebrating space exploration with its floats and balloons.

articles.title: Your last chance ever to buy one of the best DSLRs? The Nikon D850 is $600 off this Black Friday

articles.body: With many of the best Black Friday deals reserved for older mirrorless models, like the lowest price on the Canon EOS R6 II , a good digital single-lens reflex (DSLR) camera deal may go unnoticed. Luckily, we've spotted that our best DSLR , the Nikon D850, has a huge saving this Black Friday weekend, to help you save $600. You can get the Nikon D850 on sale right now at Amazon for $1,997. The Nikon D850 has entered its "end of life" stage, but only within the last few days, with the camera giant issuing a statement that it has been discontinued. With retailers now working through the last of their stock for this camera, this could be one of the last chances to buy it firsthand as stock runs down.
